analysis.one_liner: Sets federal student loan interest to zero, wipes future interest, and funds it through a new trust fund.
analysis.headline: One Senate Democrat introduced a bill to end all interest on federal student loans, picked up a single cosponsor, and it has sat in the Senate education committee since March 2026 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop all interest from accruing on existing federal student loans starting July 1, 2026, automatically rewriting the terms unless a borrower opts out, and would refinance older federally backed loans (like FFEL and Perkins loans) into zero-interest loans with no origination fees. Any new federal student loan made after that date would carry a 0% rate. It also ends the separate subsidized Stafford loan program (no longer needed once everything is 0%), raises loan limits to keep pace with inflation, and routes all loan repayments into a new Education Affordability Trust Fund whose investment returns would pay the program's administrative costs, with any surplus going to extra Pell Grants.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers — roughly everyone now repaying a federal loan and every future student who takes one. Current borrowers would stop seeing their balances grow from interest the moment the bill took effect, meaning every dollar they pay goes to principal instead of partially to interest. Borrowers holding older FFEL or Perkins loans would be refinanced into zero-interest federal loans without origination fees, and the bill is written so their progress toward existing forgiveness programs carries over. Low-income students gain a second layer of Pell Grant money if the trust fund produces surplus returns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal student loan borrowers, past and future

how_it_helps.text: Existing Federal Direct Loans would be modified automatically — no paperwork required — so that no interest accrues beginning July 1, 2026; borrowers could opt out at any time.

Borrowers with federally backed loans not held by the Education Department (such as FFEL and Perkins loans) would have them refinanced into Federal Direct Consolidation Loans that carry no interest and no origination fees, and the bill protects their eligibility for repayment plans and forgiveness by counting pre-consolidation payment history.
Every new federal student loan made on or after July 1, 2026 — including unsubsidized Stafford and PLUS loans — would carry a 0% interest rate.

All federal student loan repayments would flow into a new Education Affordability Trust Fund; investment returns would cover the program's administrative costs, and any excess could fund a Supplemental Pell Grant program on top of the existing maximum.
Annual and aggregate borrowing limits would rise each year with inflation starting July 1, 2027.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government gives up the interest income it currently collects on federal student loans, which the Treasury now counts as revenue — under federal budget rules, lending at 0% counts as a cost because the government borrows the money it lends. The bill's answer is a self-funding trust fund: repayments are invested in bonds and the returns are supposed to cover administration and eventually Pell supplements, but if bond returns fall short of that design's assumptions, the gap falls on general federal revenue — meaning taxpayers broadly. The bill also authorizes bigger, inflation-indexed loans, which increases federal lending overall.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the subsidized Stafford loan program, under which the government pays interest for low-income students during school; it is replaced by 0% unsubsidized loans with higher limits, but a named benefit for neediest students is traded for a universal one.

The trust fund's financing is speculative: administrative costs are paid only from investment returns that exceed repayments, and supplemental Pell money comes only from whatever surplus remains after that — if returns are weak, neither materializes.
Indexing loan limits to inflation could feed tuition growth, giving colleges room to raise prices knowing students can borrow more each year.
The bill lets the Education Secretary waive negotiated rulemaking — the process that lets affected parties weigh in on how major student aid changes are implemented — to speed up rollout.
Zero-interest lending benefits high-income graduate and parent borrowers as much as struggling ones, since the 0% rate and inflation-indexed limits apply to all federal loans regardless of income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and direct: millions of borrowers would stop paying interest entirely, and payments would retire principal faster. The cost — forgone interest to the Treasury — is real and the bill's trust-fund design is untested; it resembles a bet that bond returns on loan repayments can out-earn the cost of the money, which budget scorekeepers would likely treat as a substantial multi-year cost. The trade of subsidized loans for universal 0% lending simplifies the system but shifts the subsidy from targeted to universal, which spreads federal dollars up the income scale. On balance the bill is strongly weighted toward borrowers, but its financing plan is the weakest part.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate's education committee the day it was introduced and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote, with the Congress running until January 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Peter Welch introduced the bill on March 24, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
One Senate Democrat signed on as a cosponsor; that is the entire recorded support for the bill.
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — as of the latest record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet; the bill has simply gone nowhere. Borrowers keep paying interest as before, and the status quo — which produces Treasury interest income and leaves loan rules as they are — remains in place by default.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — the bill is stalled in committee

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Student Loan Interest Elimination Act on March 24, 2026.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 24, 2026, and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes or floor debates, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the bill's only two supporters in the record are Democrats, and neither party has acted on it.

industries.note: Inflation-indexed loan limits and possible supplemental Pell money would push more federal dollars toward tuition. That helps students afford school in the short run but also removes pressure on schools to hold prices down.

industries.industry: Banks and holders of FFEL loans
industries.note: The bill pays these holders off in full when a borrower's loan is refinanced, ending their ongoing interest income. Borrowers whose loans are bought out get 0% terms instead.
Loans remain outstanding and continue to require servicing, but the mass modification and refinancing of every federal loan would force a large one-time transition with added administrative work.

analysis.trajectory: With two supporters, no committee activity since the March 2026 referral, and a Congress that ends January 3, 2027, the bill is very unlikely to move. Single-sponsor education bills that sit through a session without a hearing almost always expire when the Congress ends; it would need the HELP Committee to schedule a markup and the Senate leadership to schedule floor time, neither of which has shown any sign of happening.
